text:
The front matter
---
title: "Anatomy of a lesson"
description: "One sentence. Shown on the home page and in search."
minutes: 7

Field
Used for




title
Page title, sidebar entry, home page row


description
Subtitle and the grey line under the row on the home page


minutes
The time chip, the module total and the course total


kind
The icon and colour: read, code, quiz or lab

The “By the end of this lesson you will” box









Importantminutes switches the header on



The header is only drawn on pages that define minutes. Module overview pages omit it on purpose.

title: Anatomy of a lesson
text:
A good lesson shape

Objectives (from front matter).
A short opening that says why this matters.
One idea per ## heading. Each heading becomes an entry in the right-hand outline.
A Check your understanding section with one to three questions.
A .takeaways block with two to four bullets.


  Discuss first
  If you could only keep three bullets of this lesson, which would they be? Hold that thought: it is exactly what goes in the takeaways box.

title: How the template works
section: What is generated, and what you write
text:
What is generated, and what you write
You write the lessons. Everything that merely lists lessons is generated, so it can never drift out of date.

  Discuss first
  The course home page shows a lesson count, total time and quiz count. Where do you think those numbers come from: a hand-edited list, or the lessons themselves?

They come from the lessons. Before each render, scripts/build.py reads the sidebar order in _quarto.yml and the front matter of every lesson, then writes the home page and the module overview pages into _generated/. Add a lesson to the sidebar and it appears everywhere.






NoteNever edit _generated/



Those files are overwritten on every render. Change the source (_quarto.yml, index.qmd or a lesson’s front matter) instead.

title: How the template works
text:
Where progress lives
When you press Mark as complete the lesson id is stored in your browser’s localStorage. The sidebar check, the module counters and the progress ring on the home page all read that one list. There is no account and no server, which also means progress is per browser.

  🔁 Why plain files, not a CMS?A course here is a folder of text files in git, built into a static site. That choice makes it reproducible, and it avoids what usually goes wrong with a CMS.Every change is trackedLessons are Markdown in git. Each edit is a reviewable diff, and any past version of the course can be restored in one command.One command rebuilds everythingClone the repo, run quarto render, and you get the same site. title: Project structure
text:
Reading
 5 min
A course is one self-contained Quarto website project. Copy the whole folder to start a new course.

title: Project structure
text:
One file controls the order
The sidebar in _quarto.yml is the table of contents of the whole course:
sidebar:
  contents:
    - text: "Course Home"
      href: index.qmd
    - section: "Start Here"
      href: modules/start/index.qmd
      contents:
        - modules/start/how-it-works.qmd
        - modules/start/project-structure.qmd
Reorder lines to reorder the course. Previous and next links, the home page and the module pages all follow this list.






TipName files by topic



Use project-structure.qmd, not lesson2.qmd. Moving a lesson then never means renaming files or fixing links.




Glossary
Module: a group of lessons, one folder.
Lesson: one .qmd page.
Front matter: the YAML block at the top of a page.

title: Project structure
text:
Check your understanding

  Q1. You want lesson B to come before lesson A. What do you change?
  
     Rename the files with number prefixes
     Swap their lines in the sidebar in _quarto.yml
     Edit _generated/home.md
  
  Check Answer
  



One folder = one self-contained course.
The sidebar in _quarto.yml defines the order.
Name files by topic, not by number.

title: Theming
text:
Lab
 8 min
The course has a dark theme (the default) and a light theme, and Quarto adds a toggle to the navbar. Each theme file (theme/dark.scss, theme/light.scss) only sets colour tokens; every rule lives once in theme/_rules.scss, so both themes always match. Quarto compiles them together with the Bootstrap cosmo theme.

title: Theming
text:
Colours
The palette is a handful of variables at the top of each theme file (the dark values are shown):
$sm-bg:     #05070d;   // page background
$sm-bg2:    #0a0f1e;   // panels, cards, code blocks
$sm-cyan:   #00e5ff;   // primary accent
$sm-purple: #a855f7;
$sm-pink:   #ff2fb4;
Change $sm-cyan and the buttons, links, active sidebar item, progress ring and chips all follow.






TipPanels use $sm-bg2



Use $sm-bg2 for anything that should read as a distinct panel. Using the page colour makes cards disappear into the background.

title: Theming
text:
Logo
The navbar logo is img/statmania_logo.svg. To change it:

Drop your own file into img/ (SVG is best; PNG works too).
In _quarto.yml, point the navbar at it and choose where a click goes:

website:
  navbar:
    logo: img/my-logo.svg
    logo-href: https://www.statmania.info/
The logo is shown at most 30px tall, so a wide, short image works best. To remove it, delete the logo: line.

title: Theming
text:
Footer
The multi-column footer is plain HTML in theme/footer.html: a brand column with social icons, then Courses, Resources and Company link columns. Edit the hrefs directly. Social links ship as # placeholders, so replace each # with your profile URL. To add or remove an icon, copy a line in .sm-social and pick a name from the Font Awesome brands list (for example fa-brands fa-instagram).

title: Theming
text:
Column widths
The lesson fills the window. Only the two side columns have fixed widths: the left course tree and the right rail.
$grid-sidebar-width: 290px !default;   // left course tree
The right rail width (290px) and the gutters are set in the @media (min-width: 992px) block at the bottom of the file. To keep lines readable on very wide screens, add max-width: 75rem to main.content > *.






WarningChange the grid, not a CSS width on the sidebar



Quarto lays the page out on a CSS grid. Setting width on #quarto-sidebar only resizes the box and clips the content, so edit $grid-sidebar-width or the grid block instead.

title: Theming
text:
Your turn
Open theme/dark.scss, change $sm-cyan to #facc15, run quarto preview, and watch the whole course turn yellow. Then change it back. For the light theme, change the same token in theme/light.scss.

  Discuss
  Why do you think the template defines colours once as variables, instead of writing hex values wherever they are needed?



Edit colours via the $sm-* variables.
Swap the logo via navbar.logo in _quarto.yml.
Footer links and social icons live in theme/footer.html.
The lesson column is fluid; resize the sides via $grid-sidebar-width and the grid block.
Use $sm-bg2 for panels.

title: Code blocks and live code
text:
Code
 9 min
There are three levels of “code” in a lesson, from simplest to most interactive.

title: Code blocks and live code
text:
1. Static code
A normal fenced block is highlighted and gets a copy button. Add a filename and line numbers when you want to refer to specific lines.


greet.py

def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

print(greet("Ada"))

title: Code blocks and live code
text:
2. Build-time execution
Fence with the language in braces and Quarto runs the code when it renders, then embeds the output. Learners see the result but cannot edit it.
```{python}
squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 6)]
squares
```
This needs a Jupyter install (python3 -m pip install jupyter). The demo above is left unexecuted so this template renders with nothing but Quarto and PyYAML. For R, use the knitr engine with identical syntax: {r}.

title: Code blocks and live code
text:
3. Live, in-browser execution
For a course where learners edit and run code, add the quarto-webr extension. It runs a real R in the browser through WebAssembly, with nothing to install. The rprogramming course already uses it.
---
engine: knitr
filters:
  - webr
---

```{webr-r}
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
mean(x)
```






NoteTurning this template into the R course




Copy this folder to courses/rprogramming-v2/.
Run quarto add coatless/quarto-webr inside it.
Add engine: knitr and filters: [webr] to lesson front matter (or once under format.html in _quarto.yml).
Port the old lessons: the quiz and “discuss first” markup is identical, so they paste straight in.
Copy qwebr-force-dark.js from the old course so the editor matches the dark theme.

title: Code blocks and live code
text:
Check your understanding

  Check Answer
  



Static blocks show code, build-time cells show its output.
quarto-webr makes R cells editable and runnable in the browser.
Quiz markup is shared with the old R course, so lessons port unchanged.
